qs.q: A 50-year-old presents with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, generalized oedema, and hyperlipidaemia. Which of the following clinical syndromes best matches this constellation of findings?
qs.e: The defining manifestations of nephrotic syndrome include proteinuria greater than 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia, and lipiduria. Nephritic syndrome is classically characterized by haematuria, red cell casts, and hypertension.
qs.s: Glomerular Diseases: Classification, Histology & Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with heavy proteinuria exceeding 4.0 g/day, marked pitting peripheral oedema, hypoalbuminaemia, and severe hyperlipidaemia. Which urinary finding is most characteristic of her underlying condition?
o: Fatty casts and oval fat bodies in urine
Leucocyte and granular casts in samples
Red blood cell casts and oval fat bodies
Waxy and broad renal casts in sediment
qs.e: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, and hyperlipidaemia, often shedding fatty casts and oval fat bodies in the urine. Red blood cell casts are instead a hallmark of nephritic syndrome.

ai.title: Hyperlipidaemia
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Elevated plasma lipids due to altered metabolism or loss of protein. In low‑resource settings, it often signals nephrotic syndrome, infections or malnutrition. Management hinges on treating the underlying cause and lipid‑lowering therapy.

sections.p: Hyperlipidaemia is a plasma lipid concentration above the reference range. The most common measures are total cholesterol, LDL‑C, HDL‑C and triglycerides. In resource‑limited settings, a simple lipid panel (total cholesterol and triglycerides) is often used.
b: HDL‑C <1.0 mmol/L (40 mg/dL) in men, <1.3 mmol/L (50 mg/dL) in women

t.b: Assesses baseline lipid status; abnormal values indicate hyperlipidaemia and guide treatment

sections.p: Severity is graded by LDL‑C levels, reflecting cardiovascular risk. In nephrotic syndrome, the degree of proteinuria correlates with lipid elevation.

t.b: Higher levels predict atherosclerotic risk; thresholds guide statin initiation

sections.p: In East Africa, secondary causes dominate: nephrotic syndrome, HIV, malaria, schistosomiasis, malnutrition, and herbal remedies. Primary dyslipidaemias are rarer.
b: Nephrotic syndrome – massive protein loss ↑ lipoprotein synthesis
HIV infection – viral effects on lipid metabolism
Malaria – hemolysis and inflammation alter lipids
Malnutrition – low protein intake reduces lipoprotein clearance
Herbal remedies – some contain lipid‑raising compounds

t.b: Low albumin (<30 g/L) supports nephrotic syndrome as cause
Positive smear indicates active infection that may affect lipids

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or show signs of underlying disease: oedema, skin changes, or infections. Lipid‑related symptoms are rare.
b: Fatigue – non‑specific but common in chronic disease

t.b: Look for pitting oedema, xanthomas, and signs of infection

sections.p: Baseline labs plus tests for underlying causes. When tests are unavailable, clinical judgment and simple markers guide management.

t.b: Low levels indicate protein loss; supports nephrotic syndrome diagnosis
Positive result suggests proteinuria; repeat quantitative test if possible
Positive result mandates antimalarial therapy, which may improve lipid profile
Positive result requires antiretroviral therapy; monitor lipids

sections.p: Uncontrolled hyperlipidaemia increases risk of atherosclerosis, pancreatitis, and bleeding in nephrotic syndrome.
b: Sudden chest pain – possible myocardial infarction
Bleeding – due to thrombocytopenia in nephrotic syndrome

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Lipid‑lowering therapy is added when indicated, choosing drugs with minimal renal or hepatic toxicity.
b: Supportive care – salt restriction, diuretics for oedema

t.b: Lower LDL‑C; chosen for safety in mild renal impairment
Reduce triglycerides; avoid in severe renal failure
Adjunct for very high triglycerides; safe in renal disease

sections.p: Regular lipid monitoring, repeat proteinuria checks, and lifestyle advice are essential. In low‑resource settings, community education on diet and infection control helps.

t.b: Reduces dietary cholesterol and saturated fat intake

sections.p: Nephrotic syndrome can mimic primary hyperlipidaemia; infections may transiently raise lipids.
b: Primary hyperlipidaemia – isolated lipid elevation without proteinuria

sections.p: Low albumin can falsely lower LDL‑C calculations; infections may mask true lipid levels.
b: Albumin‑dependent LDL calculation – may underestimate LDL in hypoalbuminaemia

t.b: Requires triglycerides <4.5 mmol/L; high triglycerides give unreliable LDL

faq.a: Yes, acute malaria can transiently raise triglycerides and lower HDL due to inflammation.

faq.q: What is the first drug to start in nephrotic syndrome?
faq.a: A statin (e.g., simvastatin) to lower LDL, after confirming renal function is adequate.

faq.q: How do you manage hyperlipidaemia when no lipid panel is available?
faq.a: Use clinical clues: oedema, skin changes, and basic labs (albumin, creatinine) to infer likely lipid status and treat underlying cause.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man with oedema and proteinuria has a total cholesterol of 6.5 mmol/L. What is the next step? — Treat the underlying nephrotic syndrome first; start a statin if renal function permits.
A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy presents with triglycerides of 3.0 mmol/L. Which drug is safest? — Fibrate is avoided; consider omega‑3 fatty acids.
A child with nephrotic syndrome has LDL‑C of 5.0 mmol/L. What is the target after therapy? — Reduce LDL‑C to <3.4 mmol/L.
An adult with high LDL‑C but normal albumin has no proteinuria. What is the likely diagnosis? — Primary hyperlipidaemia.
A patient with high triglycerides and abdominal pain is suspected of pancreatitis. What lab confirms it? — Serum amylase/lipase >3× upper limit.
A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops easy bruising. What is the cause? — Thrombocytopenia due to platelet loss in proteinuria.
A patient with high cholesterol refuses statins. What alternative is acceptable? — Lifestyle modification and omega‑3 fatty acids.
A patient with high LDL‑C has a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min. Which statin is preferred? — Atorvastatin or rosuvastatin at low dose; avoid high‑dose simvastatin.
